papers.title_in_file: Complex-Phase Extensions of Szegedy Quantum Walk on Graphs
papers.version_note: arXiv:2410.22011v2, 19 Mar 2025 (the record id says 2025; the file sits in the 2024 folder because v1 is from 2024).
papers.what_it_is: A quantum-walk theory paper that generalizes Szegedy's walk with link phases and local arbitrary phase rotations (the graph-phased model), gives circuits, lemmas on which coined walks it can host, a node-marking construction for search, and an O(N squared) classical simulation algorithm in the SQUWALS library.

existing.note: The paper says more than the stored value: with the single operator Us the two markings are not equal for arbitrary states (they differ by a sign on the marked self-loop states), though measurement probabilities in the computational basis agree; with the double operator Ws they are equal; and the equivalence was checked numerically on a complete graph.
existing.value: The authors show that marking nodes with a null local APR phase is totally equivalent to marking with absorbing vertices when the double Szegedy operator Ws is used; with the single operator Us the operators differ by a sign on the marked self-loop states, so they agree on states without self-loop amplitudes and give the same computational-basis probabilities, but not in other measurement bases; a simulation on a complete graph with N = 1000 nodes and M = 2 marked nodes gave overlapping curves.
existing.anchor: Section VI A, Equations 52 to 56, p.13 to 14; Figure 11, p.15; Section VIII, p.17
quotes: We have shown that marking with a null local APR phase is totally equivalent to marking with absorbing vertices in the case of using the double Szegedy operator Ws.
When using the single operator Us the same results are obtained after measuring in the computational basis, although both operators are not exactly equal.
However, this equivalence would not be valid in case we measured in other different basis.
we have simulated the Szegedy’s walk with Ws(θ⃗) and Ws′ for a graph with N = 1000 nodes and M = 2 marked nodes. The results are shown in Figure 11, where we observe that both curves overlap.
existing.certainty_reason: Derived in Section VI A from the operator forms (Equations 52 to 56) with the conditions stated, and checked numerically (Figure 11).

The O(N cubed) comparison is for building the unitary as a sparse matrix for arbitrary transition matrices.

scaling as O(N 3) in both time and memory.
Thus, the memory complexity of the algorithm scales as O(N 2).
Thus, the time complexity is also expected to scale as O(N 2).
the bigger mathematical objects that intervene are N × N matrices.

quotes: For example, if there is a small set of nodes with a different local APR phase, or there are only two local APR phases values distributed between even and odd nodes.
existing.certainty_reason: The paper's own stated limit, Section VIII, p.17.

assertions.value: The paper defines the graph-phased Szegedy walk as the most general Szegedy walk with all phase extensions: link phases φij on the edges and a local APR phase θi on each node, entering a pseudo-projector Σ whose phase rotation is R = 2Σ − 1 and whose walk operator is Us = SwR; the standard walk is recovered for θi = π and φij = 0.
assertions.anchor: Section II C, Equations 12 to 14 and Definition 5, p.3
quotes: Definition 5 (Graph-phased Szegedy’s quantum walk). It is the most general Szegedy’s quantum walk with all the phase extensions.
This operator generalizes the projector Π in (4), which is recovered for θi = π and φij = 0.
These APR phases act locally in the nodes of the graph, and the sum cannot be factorized with a projector operator.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definitions, Section II C, p.3.

assertions.value: The paper states that Szegedy's original two-reflection operator Ws corresponds to two steps of the alternative single operator Us, and calls it the double Szegedy operator.
quotes: It turns out that RA = R and RB = SwRSw, so that the original unitary operator Ws corresponds to two steps of the alternative version Us, i.e., Ws = Us2. Thus, we will refer to it as the double Szegedy operator.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's definition and its one-line derivation, Section II A.

assertions.value: The authors state that local APR phases in general need N controlled phase rotations, which is inefficient, but that when most nodes share a phase and a small set of M special nodes differ, the circuit needs only M + 1 phase rotation gates, and an even/odd pattern needs only two controlled rotations.
assertions.anchor: Section III B, Figures 3 and 4, p.5 to 6
quotes: The construction of this circuit is in general inefficient, since we need N controlled phase rotation gates.
If we have a number of special nodes M << N , there is a method for constructing the circuit only with M + 1 phase rotation gates.
if we have the same phase θe for even nodes, and the same phase θo for odd nodes, they can be implemented using only two controlled phase rotations.
assertions.certainty_reason: Circuit constructions given explicitly in Section III B with Figures 3 and 4.

assertions.value: The authors state that adding link phases modifies the update operator V; a naive method with one controlled phase gate per non-zero link phase is inefficient for N 2 link phases unless very few are non-zero or they share values, and an efficient V(φ) is possible when the phase matrix is sparse or symmetric.
quotes: In general we would have N 2 link phases, so this method would be inefficient unless there are very few link phases different to 0, or they are distributed in a manner that several phases with the same value can be applied using a common controlled gate.
if the link phases matrix φ is sparse or the distribution of phases in the graph follows some symmetry patterns, we could construct an efficient operator V (φ).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of the circuit cost and its conditions, Section III C.

assertions.value: The authors state that the update operator V must encode the N 2 transition probabilities, so its circuit scales at least as O(N 2) for a general dense transition matrix, while sparse graphs or graphs with symmetry allow efficient implementations.
quotes: In general, we need to codify the N 2 transition probabilities of matrix G, so that the complexity of the circuit would scale at least as O(N 2) for a general dense transition matrix.
For sparse graphs, where there are few transition probabilities, this operator could be implemented efficiently [30].
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of the circuit cost of its base construction, Section III A.

assertions.value: The paper states Lemma 1: a coined walk with coins Ci of dimension di has an equivalent standard Szegedy walk if and only if each coin has di − 1 eigenvalues −1 and a single eigenvalue +1 whose eigenvector has real non-negative amplitudes.
quotes: Lemma 1. Given a coined quantum walk Uc with a set of coin operators Ci of dimension di, there exists an equivalent standard Szegedy’s quantum walk Us if and only if for each coin Ci there are di − 1 eigenvalues −1, and a single eigenvalue +1 whose eigenvector has real nonnegative amplitudes.
This condition for the coins to be able to be cast into the standard Szegedy’s model is in concordance with the conditions found in the literature [24].
assertions.certainty_reason: Lemma 1 is stated with its conditions and follows from Equation 38, derived in Section IV B.

assertions.value: The paper states Lemma 2: a coined walk has an equivalent link-phased Szegedy walk if and only if each coin has di − 1 eigenvalues −1 and a single eigenvalue +1, whose eigenvector may then have any complex amplitudes.
quotes: Lemma 2. Given a coined quantum walk Uc with a set of coin operators Ci of dimension di, there exists an equivalent link-phased Szegedy’s quantum walk Us(φ) if and only if for each coin Ci there are di − 1 eigenvalues −1, and a single eigenvalue +1.
However, thanks to the link phases this eigenstate can have any complex amplitudes.
assertions.certainty_reason: Lemma 2 is stated with its conditions and follows from Equation 38, Section IV B.

assertions.value: The paper states Lemma 3: a coined walk has an equivalent vertex-phased Szegedy walk if and only if each coin has di − 1 eigenvalues −1 and a single eigenvalue −e^(iθi) whose eigenvector has real non-negative amplitudes; with local APR phases, each node can have a coin with a different eigenvalue.
quotes: Lemma 3. Given a coined quantum walk Uc with a set of coin operators Ci of dimension di, there exists an equivalent vertex-phased Szegedy’s quantum walk Us(θ⃗) if and only if
for each coin Ci there are di − 1 eigenvalues −1, and a single eigenvalue −eiθi whose eigenvector has real non-negative amplitudes.
However, thanks to the local APR phases introduced in this work, each node can have a coin with different eigenvalues.
assertions.certainty_reason: Lemma 3 is stated with its conditions and follows from Equation 38, Section IV B.

assertions.value: The paper states Lemma 4: a coined walk has an equivalent graph-phased Szegedy walk if and only if each coin has di − 1 eigenvalues −1 and a single eigenvalue −e^(iθi); the set of coins that can be cast is then maximal and encompasses the previous cases.
quotes: Lemma 4. Given a coined quantum walk Uc with a set of coin operators Ci of dimension di, there exists an equivalent graph-phased Szegedy’s quantum walk Us(θ⃗, φ) if and only if for each coin Ci there are di − 1 eigenvalues −1, and a single eigenvalue −eiθi .
Therefore the set of coins that can be cast is maximal, and encompasses the previous cases.
assertions.certainty_reason: Lemma 4 is stated with its conditions and follows from Equation 38, Section IV B.
assertions.reader_inference: 'Maximal' is within coins that are phase rotations about one vector (all other eigenvalues −1); general unitary coins remain outside the single-step model.

assertions.value: The authors state that every Szegedy walk from a classical Markov chain with transition matrix G and extended phases can be cast into the coined model, while only a restricted set of coins can be cast into Szegedy's model; for a weighted graph from normalizing an undirected graph's adjacency matrix the equivalent coin is the Grover coin.
quotes: so that all Szegedy’s quantum walk that come from the quantization of a classical Markov chain with transition matrix G and extended phases θ⃗ and φ can be cast into the coined model.
In the case that the weighted graph is obtained normalizing the columns of the adjacency matrix of an undirected graph, the equivalent coin is the Grover coin [22, 25].
If on the contrary we are provided with a coined quantum walk, only a restricted set of coins satisfy equation (38).
assertions.certainty_reason: Follows from the construction of Equations 29 to 39 in Section IV B; the Grover-coin case is attributed to Refs. [22, 25].

assertions.value: The authors show that the −1 coin cannot be cast into the standard Szegedy walk with the single operator Us, since all its eigenvalues are −1, but can be cast with the double operator Ws without any phase extension, and say more research on this is needed.
assertions.anchor: Section VI A, p.13 to 14; Section VIII, p.17
quotes: This coin cannot be cast into the standard Szegedy’s walk since all the eigenvalues are −1.

This result is intriguing, as shows that when considering the double operator the set of coins that can host is wider, not needing any complex phase extension. More research about this fact is needed in the future.
assertions.certainty_reason: Shown for the −1 coin by Equation 56 in Section VI A; the general question is stated as open.

assertions.value: The authors state that the −1 coin used for marking in the first quantum-walk search algorithm, which gives a quadratic speedup over classical search, can be cast into the vertex-phased Szegedy model by Lemma 3 using θk = 0 for marked nodes.
